conflicts.issue: 751 South Conditional 10-Year Annexation and Water/Sewer Extension Agreement (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Council split 3-4 on whether to approve water and sewer extension and a conditional 10-year annexation for the 253-acre 751 South / Colvard Farms project under threat of NC General Assembly intervention.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the conditional agreement to lock in NC 751 road widening and secure a 10-year annexation charter amendment.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell warned that state legislative leaders had stated in no uncertain terms that the General Assembly would force Durham to extend water and sewer if the city did not reach an agreement.
Without this agreement, Durham could be forced to provide utilities without developer-funded widening of NC 751 and without the 10-year annexation charter change to protect future city budgets.
Cora Cole-McFadden noted she distrusted the players but respected the Mayor's effort to salvage concessions, and Howard Clement III joined in voting yes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the utility extension and conditional annexation on planning, environmental, legal, and anti-coercion grounds.
side_b_arguments: Diane Catotti noted the request grew from 167 to 253 acres (adding Colvard Farms) without an updated cost-benefit analysis, criticized the developers' absence, and cited past protest-petition and watershed-boundary maneuvers.
Don Moffitt argued the project undermined the comprehensive plan and drove sprawl toward Chatham County instead of transit-oriented growth near Page Road and I-40.
Eugene Brown and Steve Schewel condemned General Assembly 'extortion' and refusal to negotiate with a 'gun to our heads,' warning of Jordan Lake water-quality risks.

conflicts.issue: Funding Solid Waste Fleet Replacement via Monthly User Fee vs. Property Tax (Item 5d)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 on establishing a monthly solid waste capital recovery fee to pay for sanitation truck fleet replacement, with two members arguing the flat fee is regressive compared to a property tax increase.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the monthly solid waste fee as proposed in the FY 2013-2014 budget to create a dedicated revenue stream for truck fleet replacement.
side_a_arguments: Provides dedicated funding for urgent solid waste truck fleet replacement.
Adopted as part of the balanced FY 2013-2014 budget package.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the flat monthly solid waste user fee and fund needed solid waste vehicles through the property tax instead.
side_b_arguments: A flat monthly fee on households is regressive compared to property taxation.
Both dissenting members supported purchasing the additional solid waste trucks but objected to the fee structure.
conflicts.resolution: Item 5(d) passed 4-2 as part of the Consent Agenda adoption of the FY 2013-2014 Budget, with Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel recorded as voting No.

conflicts.issue: Urban Bow Hunting of Deer Ordinance Amendment (Consent Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Council Member Diane Catotti registered formal personal disapproval of the deer bow-hunting ordinance amendment on the consent agenda while voting yes solely because state law required unanimity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the ordinance amendment permitting bow hunting of deer under state statutory framework.
side_a_arguments: Requires unanimous council support under state law to proceed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Personally oppose bow hunting of deer within city limits while declining to unilaterally veto the measure.
side_b_arguments: Registered personal dissatisfaction with the item on the record while voting yes so as not to block the unanimous requirement.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0 as part of the consent agenda.

conflicts.issue: Carolina Crossing II Seven-Story Medical Office Rezoning at NC 54 & Farrington Road (Z12-00004)
conflicts.summary: Following an 8-4 Planning Commission denial recommendation and Falconbridge neighborhood opposition to building height and severe congestion at NC 54/Farrington Road, Council debated whether $1 million in interim road improvements and a new pedestrian-crossing proffer justified approving two seven-story medical office buildings.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with $1 million in interim roadway improvements and proffered pedestrian crosswalks/signals.
side_a_arguments: City and NCDOT traffic staff verified the developer's interim turn lanes and median improvements would maintain Level of Service D and improve intersection efficiency for a decade or more before NCDOT's $40M flyover is funded.
The applicant's last-minute proffer of crosswalks and pedestrian signals addressed TTA transit rider safety across NC 54.
The site lies in a compact neighborhood tier near a future transit station node.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed by Planning Commission (8-4) and Falconbridge residents (Van Noah, Rosemary Kitchen, Julia McMillan) due to traffic congestion, cut-through volume, and seven-story scale.
side_b_arguments: NC 54 and Farrington Road is already one of the region's most congested intersections, and two medical office towers generate roughly 40 times the weekday traffic of the existing church.
Two seven-story buildings are aesthetically out of scale with surrounding one- to three-story structures and will worsen neighborhood cut-through traffic on Hunting Ridge Road.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0 after the applicant proffered pedestrian crosswalk and signal improvements at NC 54 and Farrington Road.

conflicts.issue: Living Wage Requirements and City-County Cost Sharing in Concord Hospitality Incentive Agreement (Item 12)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-1 over whether to approve a $1.33 million historic-preservation incentive for Concord Hospitality's Residence Inn at McPherson Hospital when roughly half of the hotel's permanent positions would pay below Durham's $11.91 living wage.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reluctantly approve the incentive to save the historic McPherson Hospital building, add 143 downtown hotel rooms, and gain net tax revenue.
side_a_arguments: The 1926 McPherson Hospital has no historic protection and would likely deteriorate or be demolished without the incentive.
City policy only mandates living wages for job-creation incentives and city-service contracts, not capital/historic preservation grants, and prior hotel incentives did not impose living wages.

Concord committed to good-faith local hiring via Durham JobLink, competitive benefits, and wage growth above $11.91 over time, though council members urged future policy reform on living wages and county cost-sharing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or defer the incentive unless all jobs meet Durham's living-wage standard.
side_b_arguments: Public tax dollars should not subsidize private projects that exclude service workers from a living wage.
Clement urged a two-cycle deferral to ask Concord Hospitality to incorporate living-wage compliance into the agreement.
conflicts.resolution: Incentive agreement approved 5-1 with Howard Clement III voting no.

conflicts.issue: Removal of Local Historic Landmark Designation for Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2 (Case LD1200003)
conflicts.summary: A sharp policy debate arose over whether City Council should revoke the local historic landmark designation of Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2 to facilitate a $50 million private redevelopment based on a negotiated developer-Preservation Durham compromise, overriding the Historic Preservation Commission's unanimous denial recommendation.
conflicts.side_a_position: De-list Liberty Warehouse as a local historic landmark to enable East West Partners' $50 million mixed-use redevelopment and Preservation Durham memorialization compromise, while reforming the HPC process separately.
side_a_arguments: Adaptive reuse of the deteriorated 200,000 sq ft warehouse is economically infeasible after years of failed attempts and a 2011 roof collapse.
Preservation Durham negotiated a compromise retaining the southern brick wall, northeastern facade, signs, and old wood, and documenting tobacco auction history.
Redevelopment brings $50M investment, workforce housing, Central Park connectivity, and ~$850,000/year in city real estate and sales taxes.
Landmark designation only delays demolition by one year anyway, and waiting further will not save the building.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the de-listing application under UDO Section 3.17 criteria, keep review within public Historic Preservation Commission channels, and maintain enforcement against demolition by neglect.
side_b_arguments: Liberty Warehouse remains Durham's last surviving downtown tobacco auction house and still meets cultural and architectural landmark criteria (unanimous HPC, Planning staff, and SHPO finding).
De-listing based on a developer's redevelopment proposal rather than objective historic merit undermines the entire local landmark program.
Removing landmark status eliminates binding preservation commitments and relies on private negotiations held outside public HPC review.

Critics questioned why $500/day demolition-by-neglect fines against Greenfire were stayed and argued owners should face interest/penalties when repaying tax benefits (a point Moffitt echoed for future ordinance reform).
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 6-0 to de-list Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2; Don Moffitt requested future ordinance changes to assess interest/penalties on repaid tax credits, and Steve Schewel noted ongoing Planning staff focus groups to rebuild confidence in the HPC process.

conflicts.issue: Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Grade Separations, Street Closures, and State Funding Strategy (Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Public urban-design advocates, county officials, and residents clashed with the draft Traffic Separation Study's crossing closure and concrete grade-separation proposals, while council members differed on the realism of state rail funding versus entering the NCDOT scoring pipeline.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject proposed crossing closures and concrete retaining-wall grade separations, and question the viability of state rail funding.
side_a_arguments: Durham Area Designers (Dan Jewell, Randy Hester, Eric Hite, Robin Heeks) argued concrete channels and 12-foot retaining walls would recreate a physical barrier through downtown and destroy pedestrian connectivity.
Deputy County Manager Lee Worsley warned Dillard Street closure would harm county operations and EMS response times, while Gwen Silver and James Chavis warned of isolating East Durham.
Council Member Eugene Brown argued state transportation funding is shrinking due to fuel-efficient cars and predicted light rail and grade-separation funds would remain a low-priority footnote.
conflicts.side_b_position: Treat the draft study as an initial engineering 'straw man' and position downtown crossings for state freight-rail scoring without committing to street closures.
side_b_arguments: Future freight and commuter/light rail expansion requires planning now rather than leaving downtown crossings unprotected.

Entering the NCDOT statewide freight tier (40% of state transportation funding) is the only realistic funding stream for the shared rail corridor, while reserving final decisions on closures and urban design for crossing-by-crossing feasibility studies.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 5-0 to refer public comments back to staff without endorsing long-term closures, requesting short-term safety recommendations.

conflicts.issue: UDI CDC Sewer Assessment Waiver Dispute on East Cornwallis Road (Item 11)
conflicts.summary: UDI Community Development Corporation contested a sewer assessment on 4601 Industry Lane citing P.O. Box notice issues, a prior easement swap, and pre-existing sewer access, prompting Council to defer the parcel.
conflicts.side_a_position: Waive the sewer assessment against 4601 Industry Lane (argued by UDI CDC President Ed Stewart; engineering staff confirmed UDI already had rear sewer access).
side_a_arguments: UDI did not receive mailed hearing notices sent to a closed P.O. Box and had been told an earlier easement land swap carried no cost.
Engineering staff testified that 4601 Industry Lane already had access to an existing sewer outfall and gained no additional benefit.
conflicts.side_b_position: Confirm other assessments (11B) while continuing UDI's parcel (11C) four weeks to clarify maps, easement swap history, and relief eligibility.
side_b_arguments: Council lacked maps and sufficient documentation on the land swap and whether an unconnected parcel with pre-existing availability qualifies for relief until tap-on.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 5-0 (Mayor Bell recused) to confirm Item 11B and continue Item 11C for four weeks.

conflicts.issue: City-County Interlocal Funding for Sheriff's Warrant Control and Joint Planning Department
conflicts.summary: Council members discussed Durham County Commissioners' dissatisfaction over the end of city funding for the warrant backlog program and potential county cuts to the joint City-County Planning Department, weighing independent city planning funding against preserving interlocal cooperation.
conflicts.side_a_position: If Durham County reduces its share of joint Planning Department funding over the warrant program dispute, the City should step in to fund long-range planning independently rather than let planning capacity shrink.
side_a_arguments: The city fulfilled its multi-year commitment to eliminate the warrant backlog and is doing more planning within city jurisdiction.
Under the interlocal structure, a county funding cut triggers a comparable city cut unless addressed, threatening critical long-range planning such as affordable housing around future transit stops.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid escalating an interlocal battle with Durham County government and clarify administrative communication regarding agreements.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces sufficient policy challenges from Raleigh and Washington, D.C., and needs City-County unity for all residents.
County Commissioners reportedly felt unaware that the warrant agreement had ended, indicating a need for clearer communication between administrations and elected boards.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion only; Item 20 (FY14 Planning Department Work Program) had been referred back to City Administration for revision and return in August.

conflicts.issue: Item 24: Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement — 751 South
conflicts.summary: Planning and Legal staff presented the 253-acre 751 South / Colvard Farms utility extension and conditional 10-year annexation (effective June 3, 2023), made contingent on the General Assembly passing a charter amendment extending Durham's deferral window from 3 to 10 years and requiring the developer to widen NC 751. Six speakers—Helen Fisher, Steve Bocckino, Susan Sewell, Donna Rudolph, Carolyn Aaronson, and Tom Miller—opposed the deal over Jordan Lake watershed runoff, traffic, lack of statutory authority before charter passage, and legislative extortion, while Victoria Peterson urged approval for jobs and tax revenue. Mayor Bill Bell, Howard Clement III, and Cora Cole-McFadden supported the agreement as the best way to secure NC 751 widening and charter protection before expected legislative coercion, whereas Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, Eugene Brown, and Steve Schewel voted no, citing comprehensive plan violations, the addition of Colvard Farms without updated fiscal analysis, developer absence, and refusal to yield to General Assembly threats. Catotti moved the item with the stated intent to vote no, and it failed 3-4.

conflicts.issue: FY 2013-14 Budget Revenue Strategy: Property Tax vs. Solid Waste Fee and Bus Fare Increases
conflicts.summary: During the budget E-Town Hall and public hearing, council members and residents debated whether to replace the proposed $18 annual solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass hike with a modest property tax increase.
conflicts.side_a_position: Eliminate the solid waste fee and bus day-pass increase and fund them (plus employee pay/trails) with less than a one-cent property tax increase.
side_a_arguments: Council Member Steve Schewel and speakers from People's Alliance, Durham CAN, and People's Durham argued the $18 solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass increase are regressive and disproportionately harm low-income renters and transit-dependent families.

Property taxes are progressive and federally deductible for itemizers, unlike municipal fees, and less than one penny on the tax rate could cover the bus pass, solid waste fee, Ellerbe Creek Trail, and employee pay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep property taxes flat and evaluate fee-for-service benchmarking against peer cities.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell noted that Council directed the City Manager to propose a balanced budget without a property tax increase and pointed out that peer North Carolina cities fund services through user fees rather than relying solely on property taxes.
Council Member Don Moffitt noted fees charge service users directly while property taxes spread costs across the whole community.
conflicts.resolution: Public hearing closed 7-0; final budget and fee decisions deferred to the June 6 budget work session and subsequent adoption vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting November 18, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Howard Clement III absent, the six-member Durham City Council moved efficiently through its November 18, 2013 agenda, approving all eight voting items unanimously (6-0). Council adopted the consent agenda, confirmed water and sewer assessment rolls on Ardmore Drive (granting a 20-year hardship payment plan) and Wedgewood Lane, and approved two major residential annexations and rezonings: Habitat for Humanity's Hope Crossing 2 development and the 33-lot Mineral Springs Road residential project. Council also approved a pulled appointment to the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners after Mayor Bell explained Council's practice regarding appointment deferrals.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 5, 7-18, 32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda, covering the 2014 council schedule, Rebound lease, mortgage loan servicing, employment and training grants, Church Street parking deck repairs, Human Services facility license, scrap tire recycling, vehicle-for-hire amendments, local transportation priority list, Mist Lake repairs, unauthorized water/sewer tampering ordinances, and police consulting services. Item 31 (Durham Housing Authority appointment) was pulled for separate consideration.

agenda_items.title: Mini Assessment Roll for Water Main on Ardmore Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented a reconsideration of the water main assessment at 1012 Ardmore Drive following a timely financial hardship objection. In accordance with Council's financial hardship assessment policy, staff recommended confirming the original assessment amount with a 20-year payment period at 1% annual interest.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Rolls for Water Main and Sewer Main on Wedgewood Lane
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented water and sewer main assessment rolls for completed improvements benefiting properties along Wedgewood Lane. With no council questions or public speakers, Council closed the hearing and confirmed the rolls.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Hope Crossing 2 (2800 Independence Avenue)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Stewart Engineering's request on behalf of Habitat for Humanity to annex a 0.29-acre portion of 2800 Independence Avenue and apply initial RS-20 zoning so it could be incorporated into the 29-acre Hope Crossing 2 affordable housing development. Council Member Don Moffitt prompted staff to place the required legal notification certification on the record.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: Hope Crossing 2 (A13-0004)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a Future Land Use Map amendment for the 29.9-acre Hope Crossing 2 site near Junction Road from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation. Council Member Steve Schewel asked about the location of planned city-owned additional athletic fields adjacent to the site.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Hope Crossing 2 (Z13-0011)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the companion zoning map change for Hope Crossing 2, and council members discussed future street and pedestrian connectivity to the neighboring Midland Terrace development and city park property. Applicant representative George Stancil did not speak, and no opposition appeared.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Mineral Springs Road Residential
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial PDR 4.14 zoning for up to 33 single-family homes on 9.09 acres of county enclave land on Mineral Springs Road. Council Member Diane Catotti inquired about Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission recommendations and pedestrian connections, while Council Member Steve Schewel requested offline clarification of the $165,000 net fiscal gain figure.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After recognizing Boy Scouts in the audience, Council heard a public speaker praising the nominee's integrity and dedication to homeless, low-income, and disabled residents. Mayor Bell noted for the public record that Council customarily grants any council member's request to defer an appointment, before Council moved to approve the appointment.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 5, 7-18, 32; excluding pulled Item 31)
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent. Item 31 was pulled for separate consideration (Mayor Bell initially misspoke 'Item 1' then clarified 'Item 31').
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read the headings of the consent agenda items, which included the 2014 City Council meeting schedule, Rebound lease, mortgage loan servicing, employment and training grant ordinances, Church Street parking deck repairs, Human Services facility license, scrap tire recycling, vehicle-for-hire amendments, transportation priority list, Mist Lake repairs, water/sewer fee and tampering ordinances, and police consulting services. Item 31 regarding the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners appointment was pulled from the consent agenda. Council approved the remaining consent items 6-0 with Howard Clement III absent.

votes.item_title: Item 23: Mini Assessment Roll for Water Main on Ardmore Drive (1012 Ardmore Drive)
votes.notes: Reconfirmed original assessment with 20-year payment period at 1% annual interest under financial hardship policy. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams explained that after Council originally confirmed the Ardmore Drive water main assessment on September 3, 2013, the property owner at 1012 Ardmore Drive filed a timely hardship objection within the 15-day window. Under the City's Financial Hardship Assessment Policy, staff recommended confirming the original assessment amount while allowing repayment over 20 years at 1% annual interest. No council members raised questions and no members of the public spoke at the hearing. Council approved the mini assessment roll 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Confirmation of Assessment Rolls for Water Main and Sewer Main on Wedgewood Lane
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented Item 24, requesting confirmation of water and sewer main assessment rolls for completed utility improvements along Wedgewood Lane. Staff confirmed that properties listed on the attached rolls had benefited from the new infrastructure. No council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the public hearing. Council adopted the resolution confirming the assessment rolls 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Consolidated Annexation — Hope Crossing 2 (2800 Independence Avenue)
votes.notes: 0.29-acre voluntary annexation and initial RS-20 zoning for Habitat for Humanity Hope Crossing 2 development. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented the voluntary annexation and initial RS-20 zoning for a 0.29-acre portion of 2800 Independence Avenue east of Junction Road, submitted by Stewart Engineering on behalf of Habitat for Humanity to incorporate into its 29-acre Hope Crossing 2 project. Following a prompt from Council Member Don Moffitt, Young placed the required legal notice and affidavit certification on the record for all planning hearings. With no public speakers in opposition, Council closed the hearing and approved the annexation 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Hope Crossing 2 (A13-0004)
votes.notes: 29.9-acre FLUM amendment from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Future Land Use Map amendment A13-0004 for the 29.9-acre Hope Crossing 2 site near Junction Road in eastern Durham, changing the designation from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential. Staff and the Planning Commission (11-0) recommended approval. Council Member Steve Schewel asked staff to identify the location of city-owned land planned for additional athletic fields on Attachment 2, which staff confirmed lay immediately to the east. Applicant representative George Stancil offered no formal presentation, and Council approved the amendment 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Zoning Map Change — Hope Crossing 2 (Z13-0011)
votes.notes: Companion rezoning for Habitat for Humanity Hope Crossing 2. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented companion zoning case Z13-0011 for Habitat for Humanity's Hope Crossing 2 development. Discussion focused on street and site connectivity, with staff confirming that future connectivity would link to the adjacent Midland Terrace development once constructed as well as adjacent park property. Applicant representative George Stancil declined to speak further, and no public speakers opposed the rezoning. Council closed the public hearing and approved the zoning map change 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Consolidated Annexation — Mineral Springs Road Residential
votes.notes: 9.09-acre enclave annexation, utility extension, and PDR 4.14 zoning for up to 33 single-family homes. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented the utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial Planned Development Residential (PDR 4.14) zoning for up to 33 single-family homes on 9.09 acres surrounded by city limits on Mineral Springs Road, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation and positive fiscal impact analysis. Applicant Jarrod Edens stood by the staff report. Council Member Diane Catotti asked about Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission recommendations, and staff clarified that a pedestrian connection and right-of-way dedication were committed even though non-ordinance BPAC widening requests were not proffered. Council Member Steve Schewel asked staff to follow up offline on how Budget Management Services calculated the $165,000 cumulative net gain before Council approved the item 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31 (Pulled): Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners Appointment
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up Item 31, the pulled consent item regarding an appointment to the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners. A member of the public spoke in support of the nominee, praising her honesty and commitment to working with homeless, low-income, and disabled residents. Mayor Bell remarked for the public record that when any council member raises a question and requests a deferral on an appointment, it has been Council's longstanding practice to grant that deferral. Without further debate, Council approved the appointment 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting November 4, 2013

During council announcements, Council Member Diane Catotti voiced personal objection to the bow-hunting deer ordinance on the consent agenda while voting yes solely because state law required unanimity, and Council Member Steve Schewel urged staff to explore adding Ninth Street bicycle racks under the CPGI Regency Erwin redevelopment amendment. Council approved the 16-item consent agenda 6-0 and granted water-main assessment relief until connection for three Valley Springs Road area properties 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Grade Separations, Street Closures, and State Funding Strategy (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: Public urban-design advocates, county officials, and residents clashed with the draft Traffic Separation Study's crossing closure and concrete grade-separation proposals, while council members differed on the realism of state rail funding versus entering the NCDOT scoring pipeline.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reject proposed crossing closures and concrete retaining-wall grade separations, and question the viability of state rail funding.
side_a_arguments: Durham Area Designers (Dan Jewell, Randy Hester, Eric Hite, Robin Heeks) argued concrete channels and 12-foot retaining walls would recreate a physical barrier through downtown and destroy pedestrian connectivity.
Deputy County Manager Lee Worsley warned Dillard Street closure would harm county operations and EMS response times, while Gwen Silver and James Chavis warned of isolating East Durham.
Council Member Eugene Brown argued state transportation funding is shrinking due to fuel-efficient cars and predicted light rail and grade-separation funds would remain a low-priority footnote.
disagreements.side_b_position: Treat the draft study as an initial engineering 'straw man' and position downtown crossings for state freight-rail scoring without committing to street closures.
side_b_arguments: Future freight and commuter/light rail expansion requires planning now rather than leaving downtown crossings unprotected.

Entering the NCDOT statewide freight tier (40% of state transportation funding) is the only realistic funding stream for the shared rail corridor, while reserving final decisions on closures and urban design for crossing-by-crossing feasibility studies.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 5-0 to refer public comments back to staff without endorsing long-term closures, requesting short-term safety recommendations.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting October 7, 2013

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting September 16, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: On September 16, 2013, the six-member Durham City Council (with Howard Clement III absent) issued proclamations for older workers, disability employment, Hispanic Heritage Month, and Equality Week—including a message to Durham's sister city Kostroma, Russia—and saw Mayor Bill Bell receive the Triangle Business Journal's Leadership in Diversity Award. Falconbridge residents Van Noah, Rosemary Kitchen, and Julia McMillan opposed the seven-story height, 40-fold weekday trip increase over a church, and cut-through traffic. disagreements.issue: Carolina Crossing II Seven-Story Medical Office Rezoning at NC 54 & Farrington Road (Z12-00004)
disagreements.summary: Following an 8-4 Planning Commission denial recommendation and Falconbridge neighborhood opposition to building height and severe congestion at NC 54/Farrington Road, Council debated whether $1 million in interim road improvements and a new pedestrian-crossing proffer justified approving two seven-story medical office buildings.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with $1 million in interim roadway improvements and proffered pedestrian crosswalks/signals.
side_a_arguments: City and NCDOT traffic staff verified the developer's interim turn lanes and median improvements would maintain Level of Service D and improve intersection efficiency for a decade or more before NCDOT's $40M flyover is funded.
The applicant's last-minute proffer of crosswalks and pedestrian signals addressed TTA transit rider safety across NC 54.
The site lies in a compact neighborhood tier near a future transit station node.
disagreements.side_b_position: Opposed by Planning Commission (8-4) and Falconbridge residents (Van Noah, Rosemary Kitchen, Julia McMillan) due to traffic congestion, cut-through volume, and seven-story scale.
side_b_arguments: NC 54 and Farrington Road is already one of the region's most congested intersections, and two medical office towers generate roughly 40 times the weekday traffic of the existing church.
Two seven-story buildings are aesthetically out of scale with surrounding one- to three-story structures and will worsen neighborhood cut-through traffic on Hunting Ridge Road.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 6-0 after the applicant proffered pedestrian crosswalk and signal improvements at NC 54 and Farrington Road.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting August 19, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: On August 19, 2013, with Council Member Eugene Brown excused, the Durham City Council recognized local employers participating in the Durham Youth Work Internship Program and passed the consent agenda 6-0, including the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Council confirmed a water main assessment on Duffield Road (6-0) and split an East Cornwallis Road sewer assessment item (5-0, Mayor Bell abstaining) to continue UDI Community Development Corporation's waiver request for four weeks. The meeting culminated in an extensive debate over a $1.33 million historic-preservation economic incentive agreement with Concord Hospitality for a 143-room hotel at the former McPherson Hospital (1108 W. Main Street), which passed 5-1 with Howard Clement III voting no over the exclusion of lower-wage hospitality workers from Durham's living-wage standard.

agenda_items.title: Durham Youth Work Internship Program & DollarWise Financial Literacy Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel recognized local employers participating in the collaborative Durham Youth Work Internship Program and awarded an Amazon Kindle to student Ronald Bethea Jr. through the DollarWise financial literacy program. Council Member Howard Clement III congratulated Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden, Kenneth Spaulding, and Dr. John Lucas on recent awards from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-6, 8-9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda, covering HRC and CAC appointments, preliminary assessment rolls, street acceptances, a Joint Disparity Study interlocal amendment with Durham County, Limited Obligation Bonds Series 2013A/B, a Del Webb HOA license agreement, and the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Council Member Steve Schewel commended Parks and Recreation staff for completing the 170-page master plan in-house with extensive public input.

agenda_items.title: Mini Assessment Roll for Water Main on Duffield Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff member Nathan McHenry presented Item 10, finding no qualifying relief criteria for the owner of 1205 Duffield Road and recommending confirmation of the original $2,012.50 water main assessment. No public speakers opposed.

agenda_items.title: Mini Assessment Roll for Sewer Main on East Cornwallis Road
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell recused himself due to his employment with UDI CDC and turned the chair over to Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden. UDI CDC President Ed Stewart contested the assessment on 4601 Industry Lane citing unreceived P.O. Box mailings, an earlier land swap with city engineers, and pre-existing sewer access. After engineering staff confirmed UDI already had sewer availability at the rear of its site, Council voted to approve Item 11B (confirming 1602 and 1604 East Cornwallis Road) and continue Item 11C (4601 Industry Lane) for four weeks.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development and Historic Property Preservation Agreement: Concord Hospitality (1108 W. Main St.)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD Director Kevin Dick presented a $1.33 million eight-year tax-increment-style incentive (paired with a $400,000 county grant) to rehabilitate the historic 1926 McPherson Eye, Ear, Nose and Throat Hospital into a 143-room Residence Inn, projecting a $446,000 net city return over eight years. Trinity Park and Preservation Durham leaders supported the deal, while Council Members Howard Clement III, Cora Cole-McFadden, Steve Schewel, Don Moffitt, and Diane Catotti criticized the fact that half of the 31 hotel jobs paid below Durham's $11.91 living wage and that Durham County earned far higher tax returns per incentive dollar. Council approved the agreement 5-1 with Clement voting no.

votes.notes: Confirmed original assessment of $2,012.50 against 1205 Duffield Road. Eugene Brown absent (excused).

Staff determined that no grounds existed under Council's approved assessment relief criteria and recommended confirming the original assessment of $2,012.50. No council members raised questions and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council approved the confirmation 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 11: Mini Assessment Roll for Sewer Main on East Cornwallis Road (Approve 11B; Continue 11C Four Weeks)
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell recused due to UDI CDC employment; Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presided. Confirmed 11B (1602 and 1604 E. Cornwallis Rd) and continued 11C (UDI CDC / 4601 Industry Lane) for four weeks. Eugene Brown absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell recused himself from Item 11 due to his employment with UDI Community Development Corporation, and Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presided. UDI CDC President Ed Stewart urged Council to waive the assessment on 4601 Industry Lane, testifying that UDI had closed the P.O. Box where notices were mailed and was told during an earlier sewer easement land swap that there would be no cost to UDI. Public Works staff confirmed notices were sent to the address of record in tax files, while engineering staff member Robert Joyner testified that UDI's parcel already had sewer availability at the rear and therefore gained no additional benefit from the line built for a failing neighbor septic system. Council Members Don Moffitt, Steve Schewel, and Diane Catotti sought more mapping and legal clarity on relief eligibility, leading Catotti to move approval of Item 11B (1602 and 1604 East Cornwallis Road) while continuing Item 11C (4601 Industry Lane) for four weeks; the motion passed 5-0 with Mayor Bell abstaining.

votes.item_title: Item 12: Economic Development and Historic Property Preservation Agreement — Concord Hospitality (1108 W. Main Street)
votes.notes: $1.33 million over 8 years for 143-room Residence Inn preserving historic McPherson Hospital facade. Eugene Brown absent.
votes.discussion_detail: OEWD Director Kevin Dick presented a proposed $1.33 million eight-year incentive agreement with Concord Hospitality to rehabilitate the vacant 1926 McPherson Hospital at 1108 West Main Street into a 143-room Residence Inn, projecting $1.13M in occupancy/sales taxes and $640k in property taxes for a net $446,000 city gain alongside a $400,000 county preservation grant. Preservation Durham Executive Director Wendy Hillis and Trinity Park representatives supported the incentive as the last chance to save the unprotected landmark, while public speakers Victoria Peterson and Vince Taylor demanded stronger monitoring of local and minority construction hiring. Council Members Howard Clement III and Cora Cole-McFadden objected that only half of the 31 full-time hotel jobs would meet Durham's $11.91 living wage, and Steve Schewel and Don Moffitt criticized the lopsided city-county return ($0.35 net per dollar for Durham vs. $6-$7 for the county). Though Schewel, Moffitt, Catotti, Cole-McFadden, and Bell all expressed reluctance and called for reforming city incentive policy, only Clement voted no, and the agreement passed 5-1.

disagreements.issue: Living Wage Requirements and City-County Cost Sharing in Concord Hospitality Incentive Agreement (Item 12)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 5-1 over whether to approve a $1.33 million historic-preservation incentive for Concord Hospitality's Residence Inn at McPherson Hospital when roughly half of the hotel's permanent positions would pay below Durham's $11.91 living wage.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reluctantly approve the incentive to save the historic McPherson Hospital building, add 143 downtown hotel rooms, and gain net tax revenue.
side_a_arguments: The 1926 McPherson Hospital has no historic protection and would likely deteriorate or be demolished without the incentive.
City policy only mandates living wages for job-creation incentives and city-service contracts, not capital/historic preservation grants, and prior hotel incentives did not impose living wages.

Concord committed to good-faith local hiring via Durham JobLink, competitive benefits, and wage growth above $11.91 over time, though council members urged future policy reform on living wages and county cost-sharing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose or defer the incentive unless all jobs meet Durham's living-wage standard.
side_b_arguments: Public tax dollars should not subsidize private projects that exclude service workers from a living wage.
Clement urged a two-cycle deferral to ask Concord Hospitality to incorporate living-wage compliance into the agreement.
disagreements.resolution: Incentive agreement approved 5-1 with Howard Clement III voting no.

disagreements.issue: UDI CDC Sewer Assessment Waiver Dispute on East Cornwallis Road (Item 11)
disagreements.summary: UDI Community Development Corporation contested a sewer assessment on 4601 Industry Lane citing P.O. Box notice issues, a prior easement swap, and pre-existing sewer access, prompting Council to defer the parcel.
disagreements.side_a_position: Waive the sewer assessment against 4601 Industry Lane (argued by UDI CDC President Ed Stewart; engineering staff confirmed UDI already had rear sewer access).
side_a_arguments: UDI did not receive mailed hearing notices sent to a closed P.O. Box and had been told an earlier easement land swap carried no cost.
Engineering staff testified that 4601 Industry Lane already had access to an existing sewer outfall and gained no additional benefit.
disagreements.side_b_position: Confirm other assessments (11B) while continuing UDI's parcel (11C) four weeks to clarify maps, easement swap history, and relief eligibility.
side_b_arguments: Council lacked maps and sufficient documentation on the land swap and whether an unconnected parcel with pre-existing availability qualifies for relief until tap-on.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 5-0 (Mayor Bell recused) to confirm Item 11B and continue Item 11C for four weeks.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Recognitions: National Night Out, NC Child Response Initiative, Crime Stoppers, Youth Summer Service Week, and Julius L. Chambers Memorial
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presented proclamations recognizing the 30th annual National Night Out with Police Chief Jose Lopez and honoring 30 years of Durham Crime Stoppers with board chair Pat Ellis. Representatives from the Center for Child and Family Health thanked the Police Department for nine years of partnership on the North Carolina Child Response Initiative despite recent sequestration grant cuts, and Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden recognized Youth Summer Service Week participants. Council concluded recognitions by voting 6-0 to endorse a memorial resolution for the family of attorney and former NCCU Chancellor Julius L. Chambers.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 1-16, 18-21, 23-28)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell read the titles of the consent agenda items, including minutes approval, advisory board and commission appointments, May and June 2013 bid reports, property disposition intent, a training/travel performance audit, HOME Consortium cooperation amendment, grant ordinances, ferric sulfate and Lake Michie property acquisition items, Fleet Maintenance Center roof renovations, stop-loss insurance, Old North Durham Park and American Tobacco Trail contract amendments, electronic recycling, and Bull City Connector agreement with Duke University. Items 31-35 and 39 were reserved on the General Business Agenda.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Urging the North Carolina General Assembly and Governor to Expand Medicaid
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Three Durham physicians—Dr. Gary Greenberg, Dr. Howard Eisenson (Medical Director of Lincoln Community Health Center), and Dr. Mohan Chilukuri—urged Council to pass the resolution, citing the 18% uninsured rate in Durham County and criticizing state leaders for rejecting federal Affordable Care Act funds covering over 500,000 North Carolinians. Council Members Steve Schewel and Eugene Brown spoke strongly in favor of the resolution, calling the state's refusal hostile to residents and thanking organizer Anthony Ross and local health leaders.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Street Renaming (SN1300001) — Ardmore Drive to Morningside Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young of the Planning Department presented Case SN1300001 to permanently rename approximately 150 feet of Ardmore Drive to Morningside Drive to provide a consistent street name connecting Woodcroft Subdivision to a new section of Chamberlin Subdivision. Staff reported no public comments at the May 14 public meeting and no objections from the U.S. Postal Service or reviewing agencies. No members of the public spoke at the hearing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Comprehensive Plan Amendment (A1300003) — Rustic Oaks Subdivision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case A1300003 for Rustic Oaks, LLC to amend the Future Land Use Map for a 0.66-acre parcel at 1819 Rustic Drive from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential to allow subdivision into multiple lots. The Planning Commission had recommended approval 11-0 on May 14. During public comment, a speaker performed a satirical song that included a remark about Mexicans, prompting Council Member Steve Schewel to rebuke the remark as inappropriate; the speaker apologized.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change (Z1300006) — Rustic Oaks Subdivision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented the companion rezoning case Z1300006 to rezone the 0.66-acre parcel at 1819 Rustic Drive from Rural Residential (RR) to Residential Suburban-8 (RS-8) without a development plan, allowing subdivision into approximately three residential building lots. Staff and the Planning Commission (11-0) recommended approval. There were no council questions or public speakers.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Comprehensive Plan Amendment (A1200009) — Del Webb Entry Monuments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case A1200009 by Horvath Associates to amend the Future Land Use Map from Low Density Residential to Institutional across three perimeter locations totaling 2.67 acres at the Del Webb Carolina Arbors neighborhood so entryway monuments could be constructed. Staff and the Planning Commission (11-0) recommended approval. Applicant representative Ron Horvath signed up to speak but no questions were raised.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Zoning Map Change (Z1200020) — Del Webb Entry Monuments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented companion rezoning Case Z1200020 to rezone the 2.67 acres from Planned Density Residential (PDR 3.70) to Office and Institutional with a Development Plan (OI(D)) permitting up to approximately 80 square feet of entryway signage and no buildings or other uses. Council Member Don Moffitt confirmed with staff that the site plan was submitted as the development plan, and no public speakers objected.

agenda_items.title: Scheduling of Special Meeting for Appointee Evaluations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell announced a Thursday special meeting (scheduled for 11:00 a.m., aiming to convene around 11:30 a.m.) to continue performance evaluations for the City Attorney and City Clerk, noting the City Manager's evaluation would be held at the next work session. Council Member Steve Schewel remarked to a visiting family that Council meetings sometimes feature lively debate even though this session was brief, and the meeting adjourned at 7:46 p.m.

votes.item_title: Resolution Honoring the Family of Julius L. Chambers
votes.notes: Council Member Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Following a moment of silent meditation in memory of attorney and former North Carolina Central University Chancellor Julius L. Chambers, Mayor Bill Bell requested Council's endorsement to prepare an official resolution for the Chambers family and enter it into the permanent record. No Council member offered objections or additional debate. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 39: Resolution Expanding Medicaid in North Carolina
votes.notes: Resolution shared with the Durham delegation of the NC General Assembly. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Three local physicians—Dr. Gary Greenberg, Dr. Howard Eisenson of Lincoln Community Health Center, and Dr. Mohan Chilukuri—spoke in support of the resolution, detailing how rejecting Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion leaves roughly 500,000 low-income North Carolinians uninsured and strains charity clinics and emergency rooms. Mayor Bell read the resolution noting Durham's status as the City of Medicine, an estimated 18% uninsured rate in Durham County, and projected state savings of $65 million over 10 years. Council Member Steve Schewel strongly endorsed the measure and thanked initiator Anthony Ross and the medical community, while Council Member Eugene Brown characterized the General Assembly's action as exceedingly hostile to citizens. Council passed the resolution 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Street Renaming Case SN1300001 (Ardmore Drive to Morningside Drive)
votes.notes: Renames ~150 feet of Ardmore Drive to Morningside Drive. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning Department staff member Pat Young explained that Case SN1300001 permanently renames approximately 150 feet of Ardmore Drive to Morningside Drive so the roadway connecting Woodcroft Subdivision to a new phase of Chamberlin Subdivision carries a consistent name. Staff reported that a May 14, 2013 public meeting yielded no comments and neither the U.S. Postal Service nor city review agencies identified negative impacts. No Council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the hearing, after which Council closed the hearing and approved the renaming 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Comprehensive Plan Amendment Case A1300003 (Rustic Oaks Subdivision)
votes.notes: Amends Future Land Use Map at 1819 Rustic Drive (0.66 acres) from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented Case A1300003 on behalf of Rustic Oaks, LLC to change the Future Land Use designation of 1819 Rustic Drive from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential, noting 11-0 Planning Commission approval on May 14. During public comment, a speaker performing a satirical parody song supporting the item included an ethnic joke about Mexicans. Council Member Steve Schewel immediately objected that remarks targeting ethnic groups were inappropriate even in satire, prompting an apology from the speaker before Mayor Bell accepted the comments and apology into the record. Council closed the public hearing and approved the plan amendment 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 33: Zoning Map Change Case Z1300006 (Rustic Oaks Subdivision)
votes.notes: Companion rezoning from RR to RS-8 without a development plan. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case Z1300006 as the companion rezoning to the Rustic Oaks comprehensive plan amendment, changing the 0.66-acre parcel from Rural Residential (RR) to Residential Suburban-8 (RS-8) with no development plan to enable approximately three residential lots. Staff reported that the Planning Commission recommended approval 11-0 on May 14 and found the request consistent with the Unified Development Ordinance. No Council questions or public comments were offered, and Council voted 6-0 to approve the rezoning.

votes.item_title: Item 34: Comprehensive Plan Amendment Case A1200009 (Del Webb Entry Monuments)
votes.notes: Changes 2.67 acres across three perimeter locations from Low Density Residential to Institutional. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case A1200009 requested by Horvath Associates to redesignate three perimeter parcels totaling 2.67 acres along the Del Webb Carolina Arbors neighborhood from Low Density Residential to Institutional so large entryway monuments could be permitted. Staff and the Planning Commission (11-0 on May 14) recommended approval. Applicant Ron Horvath was registered to speak but no questions were asked by Council and no opposition spoke, leading to a 6-0 approval.

votes.item_title: Item 35: Zoning Map Change Case Z1200020 (Del Webb Entry Monuments)
votes.notes: Rezones 2.67 acres from PDR 3.70 to OI(D) limiting use to ~80 sq ft signage. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented companion rezoning Case Z1200020 to rezone the 2.67 acres from Planned Density Residential (PDR 3.70) to Office and Institutional with a Development Plan (OI(D)), restricting the sites to approximately 80 square feet of entryway signage with no buildings or other uses allowed. Council Member Don Moffitt asked staff to confirm whether a site plan had been submitted as the development plan, and staff confirmed yes. With no public comments, Council closed the hearing and approved the rezoning 6-0.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 17, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council (six present, Howard Clement III absent) presented proclamations for Parks and Recreation Month, Solid Waste Employees Appreciation Day, Fill the Bus Day, and Olympic Day. Council adopted the FY 2013-2014 Budget and 2014-2019 Capital Improvement Plan via the consent agenda (6-0 overall), though Council Members Steve Schewel and Diane Catotti recorded No votes on Item 5(d), the new monthly solid waste capital recovery fee, and Council subsequently debated how Durham County's potential budget changes on warrant control could impact joint City-County Planning Department funding. Council also unanimously approved street paving on Clover Hill Place, CDBG/HOME Annual Action Plan reconciliations, the sale of 48 Southside lots, an Erwin Road right-of-way closure for Duke University, and municipal election filing fees.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations and Council Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presented four proclamations: July as Parks and Recreation Month (to Director Rhonda Parker), June 17 as Solid Waste Employees Appreciation Day (to Director Donald Long), August 3 as Fill the Bus Day (to Crayons2Calculators and Durham Regional Association of Realtors), and June 23 as Olympic Day. Council also recognized the Duke University lacrosse championship, Deputy Manager Wanda Page's appointment to the UNC Board of Visitors, and scheduled July 31 appointee evaluations.

agenda_items.title: City Manager and City Clerk Priority Items (Items 20, 29, and Supplemental Item 38)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested referring Item 20 (FY 2014 Planning Department Work Program) back to administration and referring Item 29 (East Cornwallis Road sewer main assessment roll) back for rescheduling in August, which Council approved 6-0. City Clerk D. Ann Gray requested adding Supplemental Item 38 setting filing fees for the November 2013 municipal election, which Council approved 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption Including FY 2013-2014 Budget, FY 2014-2019 CIP, and Monthly Solid Waste Fee (Item 5d)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read consent items 1 through 27 (excluding referred items 20 and 29, and reserving items 28-32 on General Business), notably including Item 5, the FY 2013-2014 Budget and FY 2014-2019 Capital Improvement Plan. Council Members Steve Schewel and Diane Catotti requested that their votes on Item 5(d)—establishing a monthly rollout solid waste capital recovery fee—be recorded as No because they viewed the flat fee as regressive and preferred funding trucks through property taxes. Council approved the consent package 6-0 with Catotti and Schewel recorded as No on Item 5(d) (4-2).

agenda_items.title: City-County Interlocal Funding Discussion: Warrant Control Program and Planning Department
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following budget adoption, Mayor Bill Bell raised concerns from Durham County Commissioners over the city's decision to end funding for the Sheriff's warrant backlog program and suggested that if the County reduces its share of the joint City-County Planning Department budget, the City could fund long-range planning independently. Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel stressed that protecting long-range planning—especially affordable housing around future transit—is essential and supported city funding if needed, while Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden noted communication gaps with commissioners and Council Member Eugene Brown urged avoiding a public conflict with County government.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Street Paving on Clover Hill Place (Dunwoody Subdivision)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robert Joyner of Public Works presented Item 28 under enabling act authority to order street paving on Clover Hill Place in the Dunwoody Subdivision from South Riverdale Drive through the cul-de-sac. No Council members or members of the public offered comments during the public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed Amendments to FY 2009-2013 Annual Action Plans (CDBG & HOME)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented formal amendments to the FY 2009-10 through FY 2012-13 Annual Action Plans to reconcile approximately $1,357,071.86 in CDBG funds and $1,699,621 in HOME funds with the city's general ledger and meet HUD expenditure deadlines. No public comments were made at the hearing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed Sale of 48 Lots in Southside
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Larry Jarvis of the Department of Community Development explained that because some homebuyers in the Southside redevelopment are not low- or moderate-income, the city must disclose terms and sell the 48 lots to homebuilders at appraised fair market value. Staff requested authorization for the sales contracts and conveyance documents. No public speakers appeared.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Street Closing of 109 Linear Feet of Erwin Road (SC1200004)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented Case SC1200004, a request by Duke University to close approximately 109 linear feet by 1.5 feet of Erwin Road right-of-way due to an existing retaining wall encroachment in front of the hospital. All internal departments and utility providers found no issues and no public speakers objected.

agenda_items.title: Supplemental Item: Ordinance Fixing Filing Fees for Municipal Office Candidates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council took up Supplemental Item 38 added by the City Clerk to establish filing fees for candidates running in the November 2013 Durham municipal election and approved it without debate before adjourning at 7:39 p.m.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Items: Refer Item 20 (FY14 Planning Work Program) and Item 29 (East Cornwallis Sewer Assessment) Back to Administration
votes.notes: Item 29 rescheduled for first meeting in August. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested two priority agenda modifications: referring Item 20, the proposed FY 2014 Planning Department Work Program, back to City Administration, and referring Item 29, the East Cornwallis Road sewer main assessment roll, back to be rescheduled for the first meeting in August. Council moved, seconded, and approved the referrals 6-0 without discussion.

votes.item_title: City Clerk Priority Item: Add Supplemental Item 38 (Municipal Election Filing Fees)
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: City Clerk D. Ann Gray presented a priority request to add Supplemental Item 38 to the evening's agenda, an ordinance setting candidate filing fees for Durham municipal offices ahead of the November 2013 election. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously approved adding the item 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Resolution Ordering Street Paving on Clover Hill Place (Dunwoody Subdivision)
votes.notes: Enabling act authority inside city limits. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Robert Joyner of Public Works Development Review presented Item 28, recommending adoption of a resolution under enabling act authority to order street paving on Clover Hill Place in the Dunwoody Subdivision from South Riverdale Drive through the cul-de-sac. No Council members asked questions and no members of the public signed up or spoke during the public hearing. Council closed the hearing and approved the resolution 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Approval of Proposed Amendments to FY 2009-2010 through FY 2012-2013 Annual Action Plans
votes.notes: Reconciles CDBG (~$1.36M) and HOME (~$1.70M) grant funds for HUD submission. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented proposed amendments to four fiscal years of Annual Action Plans (FY 2009-10 through FY 2012-13) to reconcile grant funds to the city's general ledger—approximately $1,357,071.86 in CDBG and $1,699,621 in HOME funds—and satisfy HUD timely expenditure guidelines. Staff noted the amendments were advertised in the Herald-Sun and Carolina Times and posted for a 30-day review from May 16 through June 17. With no public comments or council objections, Council closed the hearing and approved the amendments 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31: Authorization of Sale of 48 Lots in Southside
votes.notes: Authorizes City Manager to execute sales contracts at appraised fair market value. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Larry Jarvis of the Department of Community Development reported that because some homebuyers for homes built on 48 Southside lots will not be low- or moderate-income, the city was required to hold a public hearing disclosing the terms and sell the properties at appraised fair market value. Staff requested authorization to sell the lots at the indicated values and allow the City Manager to execute conveyance contracts with homebuilders. No Council questions or public comments were raised, and Council approved the authorization 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 32: Street Closing Case SC1200004 (109 Linear Feet of Erwin Road)
votes.notes: Requested by Duke University for retaining wall encroachment. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented Case SC1200004, a request by Duke University to close approximately 109 linear feet of Erwin Road by a width of roughly 1.5 feet to resolve an existing retaining wall encroachment in front of the hospital. Internal city departments and service/utility providers reviewed the request and identified no issues, and staff recommended approval. With no questions or public speakers, Council closed the hearing and approved the street closing 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 38: Ordinance Fixing Filing Fees for Municipal Office Candidates
votes.notes: Supplemental item for November 2013 municipal elections. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Following its addition to the agenda as a priority item by City Clerk D. Ann Gray, Council took up Supplemental Item 38, an ordinance setting candidate filing fees for municipal office in the City of Durham for the November 2013 election. No further discussion occurred, and Council approved the ordinance 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Funding Solid Waste Fleet Replacement via Monthly User Fee vs. Property Tax (Item 5d)
disagreements.summary: Council split 4-2 on establishing a monthly solid waste capital recovery fee to pay for sanitation truck fleet replacement, with two members arguing the flat fee is regressive compared to a property tax increase.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the monthly solid waste fee as proposed in the FY 2013-2014 budget to create a dedicated revenue stream for truck fleet replacement.
side_a_arguments: Provides dedicated funding for urgent solid waste truck fleet replacement.
Adopted as part of the balanced FY 2013-2014 budget package.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the flat monthly solid waste user fee and fund needed solid waste vehicles through the property tax instead.
side_b_arguments: A flat monthly fee on households is regressive compared to property taxation.
Both dissenting members supported purchasing the additional solid waste trucks but objected to the fee structure.
disagreements.resolution: Item 5(d) passed 4-2 as part of the Consent Agenda adoption of the FY 2013-2014 Budget, with Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel recorded as voting No.

disagreements.issue: City-County Interlocal Funding for Sheriff's Warrant Control and Joint Planning Department
disagreements.summary: Council members discussed Durham County Commissioners' dissatisfaction over the end of city funding for the warrant backlog program and potential county cuts to the joint City-County Planning Department, weighing independent city planning funding against preserving interlocal cooperation.
disagreements.side_a_position: If Durham County reduces its share of joint Planning Department funding over the warrant program dispute, the City should step in to fund long-range planning independently rather than let planning capacity shrink.
side_a_arguments: The city fulfilled its multi-year commitment to eliminate the warrant backlog and is doing more planning within city jurisdiction.
Under the interlocal structure, a county funding cut triggers a comparable city cut unless addressed, threatening critical long-range planning such as affordable housing around future transit stops.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid escalating an interlocal battle with Durham County government and clarify administrative communication regarding agreements.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces sufficient policy challenges from Raleigh and Washington, D.C., and needs City-County unity for all residents.
County Commissioners reportedly felt unaware that the warrant agreement had ended, indicating a need for clearer communication between administrations and elected boards.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion only; Item 20 (FY14 Planning Department Work Program) had been referred back to City Administration for revision and return in August.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 3, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: The marathon June 3, 2013 Durham City Council meeting featured the city's first live E-Town Hall and public hearing on the proposed FY 2013-14 budget, drawing heavy citizen opposition to a proposed $18 solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass increase alongside calls for $750,000 in supportive housing and Ellerbe Creek Trail funding. Council unanimously approved a $400,000 GE Aviation incentive package (7-0), a West Cornwallis Road rezoning (7-0), and the annual Evaluation and Assessment Report (7-0), while referring the Eno Economic Development District plan amendment back to staff (7-0) following intense resident environmental and safety objections. In the night's defining split vote, Council rejected (3-4) the 253-acre 751 South conditional annexation and utility extension agreement—with Brown, Catotti, Moffitt, and Schewel opposing Jordan Lake watershed risks and General Assembly threats, over the yes votes of Mayor Bell, Clement, and Cole-McFadden.

agenda_items.title: Welcome to NCCU Chancellor Debra Saunders-White, Juneteenth Proclamation, and Moral Monday Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council welcomed incoming NCCU Chancellor Dr. Debra Saunders-White and proclaimed June 15, 2013 as North Carolina African American Independence Day (Juneteenth). Council Member Howard Clement III requested adding a resolution to Thursday's work session in support of Rev. William Barber and the Moral Monday movement in Raleigh.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-7, 10-15)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda, including board appointments, the April bid report, a resolution opposing Duke Energy's rate increase, the Next Step Housing/CASA merger, DBAP lighting and seating contracts, solid waste and recycling contracts, parking fee changes, and e-billing vendor selection. Items 8 and 9 were pulled for separate discussion.

agenda_items.title: FY 2013-14 Proposed Budget E-Town Hall and Public Hearing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: WTVD anchor Anthony Wilson moderated Durham's first interactive budget E-Town Hall, where council members fielded questions on jobs, Ellerbe Creek Trail funding, affordable housing, police/fire pay, solid waste fees vs. property taxes, water rates, and the new police headquarters. In the subsequent public hearing, speakers urged opposing the $18 solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass increase, allocating $750,000 for supportive housing, funding Ellerbe Creek Trail, and preserving housing inspection staff; Schewel advocated a sub-one-cent property tax increase to replace the regressive fees, while Bell defended fee-for-service benchmarking.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed Bus Fare Increases
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell opened the separate public hearing on proposed DATA bus fare increases, folding in all transit comments from the budget hearing. Victoria Peterson urged generating revenue by leasing the empty second floor of Durham Station and charging Greyhound and Megabus rather than raising rider fares.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement: GE Aviation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD Director Kevin Dick presented a $400,000 performance-based incentive (paid over FY16-FY20) for GE Aviation to invest $29 million in new jet-engine manufacturing technology and create 50 jobs averaging $60,000 per year at its Miami Boulevard facility, generating $557,000 in gross new property taxes. Chamber leaders Ted Conner and Casey Steinbacher praised GE's zero-layoff record and high-school aviation academy outreach, while Victoria Peterson urged minority training and certification.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: 800 West Cornwallis Road (A13-02)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented FZH Management's request to change 0.174 acres at 800 West Cornwallis Road from Medium Density Residential to Commercial, supported 13-0 by the Planning Commission. Realtor Kim Griffin explained the lot was needed to expand parking for the Pennies for Change thrift store serving Durham Crisis Response Center.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: 800 West Cornwallis Road (Z13-03)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented the companion rezoning of 800 West Cornwallis Road from RS-10 to Commercial General. Council Member Diane Catotti confirmed that a 20-foot opaque buffer would be required along adjacent residential properties.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: Eno Economic Development District (A12-00012)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a policy alignment of Durham's Future Land Use Map with Orange County's Eno Economic Development District small area plan near I-85 and US 70. Five nearby residents (Darcy Wilson, Dr. Sarah Glass, Chris Kelsey, Joseph Henderson, and Dr. John Harvick) opposed changing rural residential land to industrial near homes, the Stony Creek wildlife corridor, and winding Old NC 10, and reported never receiving mailed notices. Expressing surprise and concern over notice and cross-county coordination, Council referred the item back to planning staff.

agenda_items.title: 2013 Evaluation and Assessment Report (EAR)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Steve Medlin presented the annual Evaluation and Assessment Report updating Future Land Use Map open-space and agriculture layers, reconciling county-approved Alexander Park, and incorporating a UNC graduate student forecasting report. Council Member Don Moffitt praised the report's quality.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: 751 South
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City staff presented a conditional voluntary annexation (effective June 3, 2023) and utility extension agreement for 253 acres (751 South and Colvard Farms), contingent on the NC General Assembly amending Durham's charter to allow a 10-year annexation deferral and requiring developer widening of NC 751. Six of seven speakers opposed the project over Jordan Lake watershed runoff, traffic, lack of legal authority before charter passage, and legislative coercion. After intense debate, Mayor Bell, Clement, and Cole-McFadden voted yes to secure road widening and charter protection, while Catotti, Moffitt, Brown, and Schewel voted no, defeating the measure 3-4.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Contract Amendment with Community Partnerships, Inc. (WIA Youth Framework)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Victoria Peterson pulled Item 8, questioning why more than half of the $175,000 budget went to staff salaries and requesting data on youth employment and GED outcomes. OEWD Director Kevin Dick explained the framework services for 140 out-of-school youth required a manager and three career counselors and exceeded federal goals; Mayor Bell directed staff to provide public aggregate numbers to Peterson.

disagreements.issue: 751 South Conditional 10-Year Annexation and Water/Sewer Extension Agreement (Item 24)
disagreements.summary: Council split 3-4 on whether to approve water and sewer extension and a conditional 10-year annexation for the 253-acre 751 South / Colvard Farms project under threat of NC General Assembly intervention.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the conditional agreement to lock in NC 751 road widening and secure a 10-year annexation charter amendment.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell warned that state legislative leaders had stated in no uncertain terms that the General Assembly would force Durham to extend water and sewer if the city did not reach an agreement.
Without this agreement, Durham could be forced to provide utilities without developer-funded widening of NC 751 and without the 10-year annexation charter change to protect future city budgets.
Cora Cole-McFadden noted she distrusted the players but respected the Mayor's effort to salvage concessions, and Howard Clement III joined in voting yes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject the utility extension and conditional annexation on planning, environmental, legal, and anti-coercion grounds.
side_b_arguments: Diane Catotti noted the request grew from 167 to 253 acres (adding Colvard Farms) without an updated cost-benefit analysis, criticized the developers' absence, and cited past protest-petition and watershed-boundary maneuvers.
Don Moffitt argued the project undermined the comprehensive plan and drove sprawl toward Chatham County instead of transit-oriented growth near Page Road and I-40.
Eugene Brown and Steve Schewel condemned General Assembly 'extortion' and refusal to negotiate with a 'gun to our heads,' warning of Jordan Lake water-quality risks.

disagreements.issue: FY 2013-14 Budget Revenue Strategy: Property Tax vs. Solid Waste Fee and Bus Fare Increases
disagreements.summary: During the budget E-Town Hall and public hearing, council members and residents debated whether to replace the proposed $18 annual solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass hike with a modest property tax increase.
disagreements.side_a_position: Eliminate the solid waste fee and bus day-pass increase and fund them (plus employee pay/trails) with less than a one-cent property tax increase.
side_a_arguments: Council Member Steve Schewel and speakers from People's Alliance, Durham CAN, and People's Durham argued the $18 solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass increase are regressive and disproportionately harm low-income renters and transit-dependent families.

Property taxes are progressive and federally deductible for itemizers, unlike municipal fees, and less than one penny on the tax rate could cover the bus pass, solid waste fee, Ellerbe Creek Trail, and employee pay.
disagreements.side_b_position: Keep property taxes flat and evaluate fee-for-service benchmarking against peer cities.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell noted that Council directed the City Manager to propose a balanced budget without a property tax increase and pointed out that peer North Carolina cities fund services through user fees rather than relying solely on property taxes.
Council Member Don Moffitt noted fees charge service users directly while property taxes spread costs across the whole community.
disagreements.resolution: Public hearing closed 7-0; final budget and fee decisions deferred to the June 6 budget work session and subsequent adoption vote.
